speaker: Andrej Karpathy
title: Skill Issue: Andrej Karpathy on Code Agents, AutoResearch, and the Loopy Era of AI
question: In applied AI, why does progress in robotics and physical-world automation continue to lag far behind software and digital agents?
guest: My view is informed by what I saw in self-driving, which was the first real robotics application. Ten years ago there were many startups, and most didn't survive long-term because moving atoms is messy and demands massive capital expenditure and time. Digital space moves much faster because bits are easy to manipulate, and we have a huge digital overhang—vast amounts of already-uploaded information that humans simply lacked the thinking cycles to process. That creates massive immediate gains in digital work. However, purely digital agents will eventually run out of already-uploaded information; at some point you have to query the universe through real experiments to learn something new. So progress follows a sequence: first huge digital gains, then the physical-digital interface—sensors feeding real-world data into models and actuators acting on the world—and finally full physical-world automation, which will lag behind even though its eventual market may be larger.

points.core: Manipulating physical matter requires far heavier capital investment than iterating on software.
points.note: Accept: atoms are harder and messier than bits, massive CapEx, or hardware/real-world deployment costs as seen in self-driving startups. Do not credit: vague claims that hardware is hard without connecting it to capital intensity or physical-world friction.

points.core: Digital agents currently exploit a massive backlog of already-digitized human information.
points.note: Accept: digital overhang of existing uploaded data, code, and papers that humans lacked the cycles to fully process, yielding immediate software leverage. Do not credit: generic claims that LLMs were trained on internet text.

points.core: Exhausting existing digital data eventually forces AI systems to run physical-world experiments.
points.note: Accept: closed-loop digital intelligence hits a ceiling without new observations from reality, creating an intermediate bottleneck in sensors or actuators bridging digital and physical worlds. Do not credit: generic claims that robots need more training data.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The core reason is data. Language and code models train on the internet's trillions of tokens, but no comparable corpus exists for physical action: robot data (forces, contacts, joint trajectories) has to be collected slowly and expensively through teleoperation or real hardware, and it transfers poorly across different robot bodies. Simulation helps, but contact-rich manipulation is hard to simulate accurately, so the sim-to-real gap persists.

Second, the physical world is unforgiving. A software agent can retry in milliseconds at near-zero cost, while a robot's errors break things or hurt people, so deployments need reliability far beyond the roughly 80–95% success rates typical of lab demos. Real environments are also unstructured and long-tailed, and this is Moravec's paradox in action: sensorimotor skills that feel trivial to humans are computationally harder than abstract reasoning.

Third, hardware and economics slow everything. Dexterous hands, tactile sensing, actuators and batteries remain costly and fragile; iteration runs at the speed of manufacturing, not of software deployment; and each robot must be built, maintained and certified, so scaling is capital-intensive rather than near-free.

Progress with vision-language-action models is real, but these bottlenecks compound.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Progress in robotics lags behind digital AI primarily because of data scarcity, physical complexity, and the high cost of real-world iteration. Digital agents train on trillions of tokens of text, code, and media scraped from the internet, whereas no comparable dataset exists for physical action, tactile force, and proprioception. Collecting real-world robotic demonstrations requires slow, expensive hardware operation, while physics simulations still struggle to bridge the "sim-to-real" gap for messy phenomena like variable friction, deformable materials, and intricate contact dynamics.

Furthermore, digital environments are discrete, observable, and forgiving: software agents can run millions of parallel trials at near-zero marginal cost, and mistakes are easily reversed. By contrast, the physical world is continuous, chaotic, and irreversible. Reflecting Moravec’s paradox, real-time sensorimotor control in unstructured spaces remains harder to generalize than abstract reasoning. Hardware also imposes bottlenecks in power, onboard compute latency, actuator durability, and manufacturing, while safety requirements constrain deployment; a hallucination in software is a recoverable bug, whereas a physical control failure risks broken equipment or human injury.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Robotics trails digital agents mainly because of data, physics, and cost. Language models learned from trillions of tokens that already existed on the internet. Nothing comparable exists for physical interaction. Robot data such as torques, contact forces and grasp outcomes has to be collected one slow, expensive episode at a time, on hardware that varies from lab to lab.

Simulation helps, but the "sim-to-real gap" stays stubborn. Friction, deformable objects, lighting and sensor noise are hard to model well. The real world is also open-ended and unforgiving. Digital agents can retry cheaply, roll back mistakes and run in parallel for almost nothing. Robots run in real time, break things, wear out, and can hurt people, so reliability standards are far higher. A 95% success rate may be fine for a chatbot but is unacceptable for a machine on a factory floor.

Hardware is another bottleneck. Dexterous hands, tactile sensing, batteries and actuators improve slowly and cost a lot, so deploying and iterating can't scale the way software does. Moravec's paradox also applies: perception and manipulation, which feel easy to humans, are computationally hard. Foundation models for robotics are narrowing the gap, but the data and hardware limits remain.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
Robotics lags behind digital AI primarily because the physical world is far harder to collect data from, simulate accurately, and iterate within. Software agents train on trillions of cheap, standardized tokens scraped from the internet and can run millions of parallel evaluations in milliseconds. By contrast, physical-world data is scarce, expensive to capture, and tightly coupled to specific robot morphologies, sensors, and environments, limiting generalization across tasks.

Simulators help, yet the "sim-to-real" gap remains formidable: modeling friction, deformable objects, lighting, and subtle contact dynamics with real-world fidelity is extraordinarily difficult. Meanwhile, physical systems face unforgiving real-time and safety constraints. A digital agent can hallucinate or retry at near-zero cost, whereas a robot's mistake can damage hardware, ruin materials, or injure people, demanding far higher reliability before deployment. Finally, progress is bottlenecked by hardware—dexterous hands, tactile sensing, battery density, and durable, affordable actuators improve on mechanical timelines rather than software ones.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Software agents learn from vast amounts of existing digital data, and developers can run thousands of tests in parallel, reset the environment, and roll back many mistakes. Robots need data about how physical actions play out. Collecting it takes hardware, time, and often human supervision. A grasp that works on one robot or in one room may fail with a different gripper, lighting, or surface. Simulation helps, but it’s hard to model contact, friction, and flexible objects accurately enough for every situation.

Robots also have to turn predictions into precise movements in real time despite noisy sensors, worn parts, and people moving nearby. A rare failure can break equipment or injure someone, so deployment requires extensive testing and safeguards. Each installation can also bring integration and maintenance costs. That’s why robots scale fastest in structured settings like factories, where the work and surroundings can be made predictable.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Robots face a harder learning problem and a higher cost of failure. A software agent often works through an interface that tells it what actions are available and whether they succeeded. A robot picking up a glass has to infer its position from imperfect sensors, judge how firmly to grip it, and adjust as it starts to slip. A small error can break the glass.

Digital tasks can often be copied, run in parallel, and reset cheaply. Real-world trials take time, wear out hardware, and sometimes put people at risk. Simulation speeds up training, but it can miss details such as friction and how objects deform on contact.

Those differences help explain why factory robots excel in carefully arranged workcells while household robots still struggle. A demonstration can succeed under favorable conditions. A useful product has to work safely and affordably across thousands of variations.
